title: Agent Inventory vs. CMDB
summary: A CMDB confirms an agent exists. It has no column for permission scope, and its own health metrics cannot detect an agent whose access changed while the record stayed still.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**A CMDB will confirm an agent exists. It has no column for what the agent is allowed to do, and its own data-quality machinery cannot notice when that changes.**


ServiceNow measures CMDB health on three KPIs: completeness, which checks whether required and recommended attributes are populated; correctness, which looks for duplicates, orphans and stale records, with a default staleness rule at 60 days; and compliance, which audits records against templates. Every one of those inspects a stored value. An agent whose granted scopes doubled last Tuesday changed none of its attributes, so its record scores perfectly healthy.


The usual fix is bolting custom attributes onto an existing configuration-item class. That works for infrastructure that sits still. It fails on agents for a structural reason: under MCP, a server's tool set "MAY vary by the authorization presented on the request", so an agent's real capability surface is a function evaluated per call, not an attribute you can store and audit.


None of this makes the CMDB wrong. It is still the best record of what you operate, and rebuilding its dependency graph would be waste with a new name on it.


What to do today: keep the CMDB, add a second record for actors, and make the link a field. The inventory points at configuration items; the configuration items point back.
